(p-200)Surah al-Fil (The Elephant)

Makkiyyah (Meccan), and its verses are five.

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ The address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the interrogative hamza serves to affirm his seeing by negating its absence. "Kayfa" (how) is suspended from the verb of seeing (ta'liq) and is in the accusative by what follows it. The seeing is cognitive (ilmiyyah), meaning: "Have you not known with firm knowledge, approaching direct witnessing and observation, through hearing the widely transmitted reports and observing the manifest traces?" The suspension of seeing to the manner of His action, mighty and majestic, rather than to the act itself, as in saying "Have you not seen what your Lord did...", is for the magnification of the event and to announce that it occurred in a awe-inspiring manner and a wondrous form, indicating the greatness of Allah's power, the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom, the might of His House, and the honour of His Messenger ﷺ. Indeed, this is among the preliminary signs (irhasat) of what is narrated: that the story occurred in the year in which the Prophet ﷺ was born.

Its details: Abraha ibn al-Sabbah al-Ashram, king of Yemen on behalf of Ashama al-Najashi, built a church in San'a and named it al-Qullays, and he wished to divert the pilgrims to it. A man from Kinanah went and sat in it at night, and that angered him. It is also said that a group of Arabs lit a fire which the wind carried and burned it, so he swore that he would demolish the Ka'bah. He set out with his army, and with him was an elephant named Mahmud, which was strong and huge, and twelve other elephants besides it. It is said there were eight, and it is said there were a thousand, and it is said he had only that one. When he reached al-Mughammas, Abd al-Muttalib went out to him and offered him a third of the wealth of Tihamah in return for turning back, but he refused, arrayed his army, and advanced the elephant. Whenever they directed it toward the Haram it knelt and would not budge, and whenever they directed it toward Yemen or any other direction it ran. Then Allah sent birds, black, and it is said green, and it is said white, each bird carrying a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet, larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea. The stone would fall upon a man's head and come out through his anus, and each stone bore the name of the one it would strike. They fled and perished on every road and watering place. It is narrated that Abraha's fingertips and joints fell off, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart. His vizier Abu Yaksum escaped, with a bird hovering above him until he reached the Negus and recounted the story to him; when he finished, the stone fell upon him and he dropped dead before him. It is also said that Abraha had seized two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib, so he went out to him concerning them. When Abraha saw him, he was great in his eyes, for he was a handsome, tall man. It was said: "This is the chief of Quraysh and the leader of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountaintops." So Abraha descended from his throne and sat on his carpet. It is also said he had him sit with him on his throne. Then he said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" When he mentioned his need, he said: "You have fallen from my eyes, having come to demolish the House which is your religion and the religion of (p-201) your fathers, and your protection and your honour since ancient times, and you do not speak to me about it. Have the camels that were taken from you distracted you?" Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." Then he returned, came to the door of the Ka'bah, took hold of its ring, and with him a group of Quraysh, supplicating Allah, mighty and majestic. He turned while praying and behold, there was a bird from the direction of Yemen. He said: "By Allah, it is a strange bird, neither Najdi nor Tihami." Then he let go of the door-ring and went off with his companions, waiting to see what Abraha would do. Allah sent the birds upon them, and what happened happened. It is also said that Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. It is narrated from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "I saw the driver of the elephant and its keeper, both blind and crippled, begging for food."

It is read "Alam tar" with the ra' sukun, for the sake of emphasis in showing the trace of the jussive particle.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 105, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did He not make their scheming go astray?﴾ ...etc. is a general statement of what Allah, may He be exalted, did to them. The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for affirmation (taqrir), as has already been explained. For this reason, what follows is conjoined to the interrogative clause, as if it were said: He has made their scheming, in the disabling and destruction of the Ka'bah, come to nothing and ruin, by destroying them with the most hideous destruction.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾

**Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 105, verse 3:**

﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾, i.e., groups and companies. It is the plural of "ibala" (إبالَة), which is a large bundle (of sticks or fodder). The group of birds was likened to it because of how they were pressed together. It has also been said: "ababil" is like "aba'abid" and "shamatit," having no singular form of its own.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 105, verse 4:

﴿تَرْمِيهِمْ بِحِجارَةٍ﴾ ("They strike them with stones") is an attribute (sifah) of "ṭayran" (birds). It is also read as "yarmīhim" with the masculine form, because "ṭayr" is a collective noun (ism jam') whose feminine gender is taken in terms of meaning (bi-i'tibar al-ma'na).

﴿مِن سِجِّيلٍ﴾ ("of baked clay") means: of hardened clay (min ṭīn mutaḥajjir). It is an arabicized word (mu'arrab), originally Persian, "sang-gil" (sankak kil). It was also said that it is as if it were a proper name (ʿalam) for the register (diwan) in which the punishment of the disbelievers was written, just as Sijjin (ʿalam) is the name of the register in which their deeds are written. It is as if it was said: "with stones from among the punishment that is written and recorded." Its derivation is from al-ʾisjāl (ʾisjāl), which means sending down (al-irsāl).

Verse 5: ﴿So He made them like stripped stalks [or: like a field of crops] eaten up.﴾ Hmm, need to render the Arabic faithfully per instructions.

Translation:

﴿So He made them like chewed-up husks﴾ like the leaves of a crop in which the eating has taken place, which is when the worms have eaten it, or its grain has been eaten so that it remains empty of it; or like chaff that has been eaten by animals and trodden down, [the verse] pointing to its initial state.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Fil, Allah will protect him during the days of his life from being swallowed up by the earth and from being transformed." And Allah knows best.
